utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Dr. Idriz Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the parties are informed of today's -- as of today's sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Merdzanic. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Merdzanic is my last name, and Idriz is my first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, as we discussed, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing, and we first need to deal with the formalities associated with that submission. You've testified in three trials before the ICTY, and in particular, the Stakic trial on the 10th and 11th of September, 2002. On the 12th of September, 2002, did you provide a handwritten document to the Tribunal regarding your Stakic testimony?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have 65 ter 23496 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that's on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I have written.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness. Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, does this clarify an issue in your Stakic testimony in relation to the check-points in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct. There was one question whether there was a check-point at the entrance into Kozarac, and I thought about that after the trial, and I remembered that there was an obstacle there for this tank that was at the crossroads near the entrance into Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, have you had the opportunity to review the audio recordings of your Stakic testimony?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is one word at transcript page 7769, line 16, when he was asked in chief about the film that was taken about the time at Keraterm, and the word "Keraterm" should read "Trnopolje."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you agree with that correction, Dr. Merdzanic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It is correct. I was never in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With those clarifications, the document that you see on the screen and the one that we just spoke about, can you confirm that your Stakic testimony accurately reflects your statements at the time?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that along with an explanation that I'd like to provide. When I read this, I noticed that the time between the announcement of the journalists' visit and the arrival of the International Red Cross, it was sort of unclear. I would like to clarify that. When it was announced that journalists would arrive and then up until the arrival of the International Red Cross, hundreds of persons were killed and I think that that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say hundreds of people were -- were killed, can you elaborate on that, please?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you'll allow me to explain it now, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you indicate first, Ms. Sutherland, what part -- what pages are dealing with that part, the interval between the announcement and the arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the arrival of the journalists -- the first visit of the journalists starts on page 7793.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That's sufficient. Why don't you proceed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. -- Dr. Merdzanic, when you say that a large number of people were killed, can you elaborate on who you were actually referring to.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Camp inmates. When Dr. Karadzic promised in London that he would allow journalists to visit the camps because he had claimed that they were no camps, he returned to Bosnia and then an order arrived from Pale from Dr. Karadzic to have the camps prepared for the journalists' visits. Until the camps were prepared, the journalists could not come. This order for the camps to prepare for the visits was basically a death sentence for many camp inmates. As for the Keraterm camp, it was decided to have it completely emptied and to have all the camp inmates removed. Since there were a great many camp inmates, they didn't know what to do with them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Did you mean Keraterm camp? Did you not say that you have never been to Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking about the Keraterm camp because it's tied to Trnopolje, because part of these people came to Trnopolje. So I'm speaking along those lines. You can understand only if all three camps are explained together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, so you indicated earlier that there were a large number of people killed, and you have just provided an answer then to say that this order for the camps to -- to be prepared for the visits was basically a death sentence for many camp inmates. Can you -- can you just elaborate on -- on what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to explain that briefly now. They reached a simple decision for Keraterm. Part of these people were supposed to be transferred to Trnopolje. As for one hangar, they simply put machine-guns in front of the door to that hangar, and they killed everybody who was inside. Crljenkovic Enes was the only person to survive. He is alive to this day. Everybody else was killed, over 100 people. Some people were taken in an unknown direction. That is as far as Keraterm is concerned. Omarska was also supposed to prepare for the arrival of the journalists. Some people were sent to Manjaca. That is a camp that was at the military barracks in Manjaca. Before they handed them over, they killed some of them. Women and minors were first sent to Trnopolje. Some of the inmates were hidden somewhere, taken away on buses and trucks, and then after the journalists left, they were brought to Trnopolje; whereas some persons were taken away in an unknown direction, and to this day their bones are still being discovered in the places where they were killed. For a small number of people they prepared military cots with bed linen, food, and those are the people they showed to the journalists. Now, as far as Trnopolje is concerned, let us try to link all of this up and see why I'm putting it this way. In Trnopolje, people knew for quite a while that the journalists would come to visit the camp, and since Trnopolje was already full, they organised convoys so that the camp could be emptied, at least halfway, so that inmates from Keraterm and Omarska would have room there. The women and children who had arrived from Omarska were released, taken to Prijedor. A fence was put up between the shop for construction material and the other house on the other side, and that is where they put these people. All the women and children practically -- the women and children from Trnopolje were practically taken away in a convoy, and that was the first time that they allowed men to leave in that convoy. This is not the convoy that was taken to Vlasic. That was a convoy before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, the -- the evidence that you're just giving now about the fence that was put up is -- is dealt with in your Stakic testimony, so we won't go over that again now. So with that clarification that you've just given, if you were asked about the same matters here in court today that were discussed with you in the Stakic -- that you gave evidence about in the Stakic case, would you provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's the same information except that this convoy for Vlasic was organised when Dr. Karadzic allowed the camp of Trnopolje to be taken over by the International Red Cross. Before they arrived, they organised a big convoy in order to reduce the number of inmates even more. So when the International Red Cross arrived, there were a lot less inmates, whereas those who were sent via Vlasic were taken out of this convoy and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And again, Dr. Merdzanic, with that additional clarification, if you were asked about the same matters here in court today as you were -- you gave evidence about in the Stakic case, would you provide the same information, that is, even if you couldn't give it word-for-word, the essence of your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same. However, having said that, this was based on the order from Pale and Dr. Karadzic, namely, to prepare these camps for the arrival of the journalists and for them to be cleansed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 22174A, which is the English transcript of Dr. Merdzanic's testimony. And I note in the English transcript there's an incorrect spelling of the name Sahuric on transcript pages 7739, 7826, and 7860. It should be spelled S-a-h-u-r-i-c. And there is also a mistake in the transcript at page 7779, lines 21 to 22. There's a reference to Exhibit S15-41 and that should be S15-14, which is already Exhibit P00602 in our case. I also seek to tender 65 ter 22714B, which is a redacted public version of the witness's Stakic testimony, and 65 ter 23496, which is the handwritten correction which the doctor provided at the completion of his Stakic testimony. I would seek to tender those three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just three documents being transcript and redacted version and what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then this -- this document that Dr. Merdzanic recognised this morning, which was put up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Now I understand. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be all admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 22174A will be Exhibit P3880, under seal. 22174B will be Exhibit P3881. And 65 ter 23496 will be Exhibit P3882.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before going further, Ms. Sutherland, you stated that had what Mr. -- Dr. Merdzanic said this -- today was covered in his Stakic testimony, but my understanding is that it is true that he said that camp, Trnopolje camp was prepared for the arrival from Keraterm, but he didn't say at that time as to the killing at the Keraterm itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was specifically referring to the fence that is -- that is dealt with in his Stakic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, actually we didn't object or interrupt the witness, but would I hope that you could take that in consideration if Dr. Karadzic needs some additional time for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see how it will evolve. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And with Your Honours' leave, we'll read a summary of the witness's written evidence. Dr. Idriz Merdzanic, a Bosniak, lived in the Prijedor municipality from 1988 until he was detained at the end of May 1992. In 1989, he began working as a physician in the Prijedor Health Centre, which was responsible for health clinics in the municipality. In 1991, the witness was in charge of the Trnopolje outpatient clinic and in mid-1991 was also assigned to the sawmill in Kozarac where he was in charge of treating employees of that company. Dr. Merdzanic testified about the arming of the Serb population and the distribution of weapons by the JNA in early 1992. He testified about the increase in Serb military forces and the establishment of check-points in the area. The witness testified that he heard about negotiations concerning the Kozarac police force which were led by Stojan Zupljanin. The Kozarac police were given an ultimatum to accept the Serb insignia and fly Serb flags in Kozarac by a certain date, otherwise the army would take Kozarac by force if the conditions were not met by the stipulated dead-line. When the ultimatum expired, people were no longer allowed to leave Kozarac. The witness described the attack on Kozarac on the 24th of May, 1992. The shelling lasted for two days. During this attack the witness treated people for injuries received from shelling and infantry weapons. The witness contacted the military command that was attacking Kozarac and asked for permission to evacuate two seriously wounded children that were dying. The reply he received was, quote, "Let all of you Balija die there. We will kill you anyway." A number of people died as a result of injuries received during the attack. And this is scheduled incident A 10.1. On the 26th of May, 1992, the witness was taken from Kozarac to the Trnopolje camp, which is scheduled detention facility C 20.4. Along with many of the men, women, and children, he was taken to Trnopolje -- he was taken to Trnopolje that day. The witness remained in the camp until 30th of September, 1992. Dr. Merdzanic testified about the inhumane conditions including lack of adequate food or hygiene, beatings, rapes, and several killings, and this is schedule incident B 15.5. He described how he treated detainees for dysentery, body lice, scabies, and hepatitis, all of which are consistent with extremely unsanitary conditions. He testified that he reported incidents of rape to the camp authorities. The witness testified that all around Trnopolje camp there were guard posts with guards. The wire fence was put up at Trnopolje to contain prisoners from Keraterm and Omarska, and after the first visit of journalists, which included Penny Marshall, the fence was taken down. Dr. Merdzanic also described the second visit to Trnopolje camp by Penny Marshall and a visit by the ICRC in August 1992. The witness testified that when the buildings at Trnopolje were filled to capacity and could no longer hold any more people, the first convoy of women, children and elderly men was organised. Continuing the forcible removal of non-Serbs from their homes in the area surrounding Trnopolje led to an increase in the detainee population in the camp. The witness gave evidence about the convoy that left Trnopolje camp and went over Mount Vlasic. Later the witness heard that younger men were taken off the convoy and killed on Mount Vlasic. And this is scheduled incident B 15.6. Prior to leaving the camp on a convoy on the 30th of September, 1992, the witness and others had to sign certificates to the effect that they were abandoning all their property to the Serb authorities. That completes the summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, I just have a limited number of questions for you. You worked at the Prijedor Health Centre in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... all belonged to Prijedor. I was officially employed in Prijedor but my clinic was in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was the employment of non-Serbs terminated after the takeover of power by the Serb authorities? And here I'm specifically referring to persons in the hospital who worked in the Prijedor Health Centre.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were first dismissed from the health centre. They were summoned to come to work and the director of the health centre, Dr. Dereta [phoen] lined them up in the corridor at the entrance and told them that from that day on, they are no longer allowed in the building and shouldn't come to work again. The same happened to the Muslim workers at the hospital in Prijedor a day or two later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 18897 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, this is a list of 114 names, and this is a document that you recently reviewed. It's a list of employees whose employment has expired and it lists a number of -- of doctors and other staff from the general hospital Prijedor and the dates of when their contract was expired. Do you know a number of these persons listed on this list?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The staff is mixed also with the staff from the hospital and the health centre. I know only a smaller number of them. I was not born in Prijedor. I moved there in 1988, and I was working more in the field. I didn't know personally most of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you know why the employment was terminated of the people that you do know on this list?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They were all either Muslim or Croat. At that time, I was already in Kozarac, and as far as I know, the only reason for their termination was that they were Muslims, and most of them did not agree to be mobilised and go to the war zones in Croatia. I'm not aware of any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did your wife also work at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: My wife worked at the health centre, and she was in that group of personnel to whom Dr. Dereta said that they should not come to work any more. They were prohibited from coming to work anymore, and that was without any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And are you able to read out the number of the -- next to the names of the doctors that you -- that you are familiar with on this list? Or doctors and other staff.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: For instance, number 46, Dr. Esad Sadikovic. He was involved in those negotiations, and then when their army occupied Prijedor, he was taken to Omarska and killed. Then Dr. Zeljko Sikora was also taken to Omarska, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I also heard of Islam Bahonjic, but I'm not sure what became of him. Dr. Emir Keric, I know him as well. Number 91, it says Emir Henim, in fact it's Henic. I know the man. Then Dr. Zoran Vikalo. He's a Serb doctor. And it's interesting, then, when the forced mobilisation was going on, he was hiding and later fled to Croatia to avoid mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dr. Majda Sadikovic, and I know also Dr. Ibrahim Henic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you also know Dr. Begic who worked at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know him. He was a surgeon, and he worked for a while in the hospital even after the takeover as long as they needed him, but when they no longer needed him, they took him to Omarska and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the associated exhibits, and in relation to the videos, I have the time-codes. I don't know whether you want me to read them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that needs to be tendered as 65 ter 40424C. The time-code is 00:31:31 to 00:32:03.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a couple of further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. There's one other video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 65 ter 40470 is -- needs to be referred to as 40424C -- 404, sorry, 70C, and the time-code for that is 00:05:38 to 00:06:17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to 65 ter numbers, starting from 20535 to 20537, i.e., three documents containing two photos each, from the transcript and the photos itself, it's not clear what these photographs testify to in terms of relevance and probative value. If you could explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could -- if I can actually just quickly deal with them with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 20535 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, you were shown this photograph in the -- during your Stakic testimony.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct. We made those photographs with the camera that belonged for -- to Arap Gulasovic [as interpreted] and they were made in Trnopolje at the clinic the first day when we came. The top photograph shows Mujo, the technician. Next to him is a man who was a patient. He just spent there one night. And the photograph below shows me and Dr. Dzonlagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that Hase Dzonlagic on the left and you on the right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Hase Dzonlagic is on the left and I am closer up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in your answer you said that these were photographs with the camera that belonged to -- and the name in the transcript is -- is -- were you referring to Azra Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I already said it belonged to Azra Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And these photographs were taken early in the days of being at Trnopolje camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go through the other document --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] If could I have 65 ter 20536 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise that -- those photographs?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They are also from Trnopolje. Below you see Azra Blazevic, and the one at the top is Sefik. I forget his last name, but I did state it in my previous statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sefik Karabasic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct. Sefik Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he was also working with you in the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't think he worked at the health centre. He only joined to help us during the shelling in Kozarac, and he came with us to Trnopolje from Kozarac. I don't know what his normal occupation is because I didn't know him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he was with you in the clinic at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a photograph from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that was where you -- you had to -- you slept in the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We also slept there. We had everything there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If could have 65 ter 20537.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The one at the top shows a nurse, that's also in Trnopolje, and below is Gutic Vasim [as interpreted], a student of medicine, and next to him is Goga, who came with us to Trnopolje, but she was Serb, and the Serbs told her she couldn't stay. She had to go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the gentleman that you mentioned that -- that is on the right of the photo, the name again in the transcript, is that Vasif Gutic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Vasif Gutic, who was a student of medicine then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And of these three photographs, are they simply putting faces to names that you testify about in your transcript as -- as persons that were with you in the medical centre at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender those photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to 65 ter 20743, which is a diagram drawn by the witness depicting Trnopolje camp, I think we need an English translation. Until -- until then, we'll mark it for identification. Then one final matter is related to 65 ter 40469A, which is an excerpt from serial dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The time-code for that video is 00:09:00 to 00:09:41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, however, did the witness recognise the place show -- shown in the video? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can -- we could play that clip very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's -- it's 30 seconds long. Or 45 -- 41 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need to switch to Sanction. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Reid has it ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "But not everything is normal. There is evidence of what has happened. Along the main road. These are burnt-out Muslim homes. The cross in a circle is a Serb's way of marking them out for special attention. This is ethnic cleansing with a vengeance, and it was thorough."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, did you recognise the -- the houses in the footage that you just saw?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, not 100 per cent, but I believe that is a part of Kozarac next to the main road that goes from Prijedor to Banja Luka. But again, I'm not sure because the picture is very dark, and the houses were not so completely destroyed when we were leaving Kozarac, but I believe that's the lower part of Kozarac, closer to the Banja Luka-Prijedor road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit that, including that, then all the -- with the -- all the clarification and all the associate exhibits will be admitted into evidence and given number in due course. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I -- just so that we're on the same wavelength that the Chamber would not be giving any weight to the commentary that was in that video other than the commentary that the witness has given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Instead of starting the cross-examination now, we'll take the break now, and we'll resume at 20 -- yes, half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As indicated by Ms. Sutherland, Dr. Merdzanic, your testimony given in the previous case was admitted in its entirety in lieu of your examination-in-chief. Now you'll be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon, Excellency. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since our time is short, I'll try to put questions that are as clear as possible, especially with regard to matters we can easily agree upon. So most of your answers can be a simple yes or no. Of course, I am not restricting you in any way. In every one of your testimonies, did you take an oath stating that you would say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you testify, do you adjust your testimony to the person who stands accused?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, but emphasis is laid on the person who is accused, so then perhaps one can emphasise things that are the responsibility of the person who is accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is it that indicates that to you, what you're supposed to emphasise?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm over 18. I'm of age, and I think that I can make my own decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you do make a selection after all. You do adjust things, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As for my view of the situation, that is what I present here. The Judges are here to hear all the parties, collect evidence, and rule. So this is just what comes from my side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come you never mentioned that my order was a death sentence for hundreds of people?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was not -- I was not asked directly, and it was not your trial. This is the first time that I'm attending your trial, and you decided to have these camps prepared for the arrival of the journalists, and I was there, and I saw how these camps were being prepared for the arrival of the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that I ordered something?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's quite simple. It's only logical. In principle --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. Let us agree that you should say only what you know, not what is logical. Do you know? Did you see my order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you asked how he did know that you ordered something. Then you should hear him out. Don't interrupt the witness, please. Dr. Merdzanic, could you repeat your answer or start it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, that is quite logical. Dr. Karadzic promised journalists that he would let them visit the camps. The journalists came to the camps through Karadzic in Pale. Those who held the camps had no idea about that. The only way they could find out that journalists were coming was if Karadzic sent them that information from Pale. Nobody else could give that kind of information. I said what he had ordered. I'm not going into whether he had issued precise orders to have these persons killed or not. I'm just saying that that decision meant a death sentence for the camp inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any order of mine? Let me put it that way then. Did you see any order of mine in that respect?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see any order of yours, but I'm intelligent enough to be able to reach certain conclusions. I know how much 2 plus 2 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, Doctor, you know that in medicine also people have to reach conclusions on the basis of facts. So I kindly ask you to give answers about what you know.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I have just given you an answer based on facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you not say earlier on that hundreds of people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: People knew earlier on as well that in Keraterm an entire hangar had been killed and that people were killed in Vlasic. That was discussed sufficiently, most definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before both of you continue. Dr. Merdzanic, since you're speaking the same language and both of which are to be interpreted, if you could pay attention sufficiently to put a pause between you start answering the question. I appreciate your kindness. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were not in Keraterm, and you did not see these killings; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was not, but after being in camp, I talked to Enes Crljenkovic who survived all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today on page 9 you said that on the basis of my order or information to the effect that journalists would come and the International Red Cross, a convoy went to Vlasic and these people were killed there; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, on page 9, that that was done in order to reduce the number before the Red Cross arrives; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Before the International Red Cross arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the International Red Cross arrived on the 15th of August?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the killings were committed on the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I cannot say now. I don't have this information when this happened exactly. This convoy left before the inmates were registered by the International Red Cross. The International Red Cross had not arrived yet, had not registered these inmates yet, those who were taken to Vlasic and killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether these dates are correct: The 15th of August, the Red Cross visited, and the 21st of August, the crime at Koricanske Stijene was committed. Is that right yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know when the crime was committed at Koricanske Stijene. I just know that the International Red Cross had not registered these people yet. They appeared on the 15th, but this convoy had left before the International Red Cross arrived and managed to register these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today the distinguished Madam Sutherland interpreted your positions on page 12 that the ultimatum to Kozarac was issued because of the flag and the insignia on police caps; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did not attend these meetings. Now, whether that is the way it was exactly -- well, at any rate, the policemen in Kozarac opposed that. They did not want to recognise the Serb authorities, and they did not allow the Serb police to take over Kozarac, where the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the conflict in Kozarac broke out because of the flag and insignia?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, the conflict did not break out on account of that. The conflict broke out because the Serbs wanted to take Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they want to take Kozarac because of the flag and insignia or because of something else?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, it was of great strategic importance for them to create a great ethnically pure Serbia. That was the real reason. The insignia were probably just a pretext or an excuse for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Zupljanin wrote that Kotor Varos and Prijedor do not have to use these insignia?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I know that they attacked Kozarac and got the tanks out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 14 - and could we please call this up now, P3883 - you spoke about the list of persons whose employment had terminated. Do you know that termination of employment is one thing and dismissal is another?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: These persons were forbidden from coming to work any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who can confirm what you're saying just now?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: My wife can. She was there personally, and those were the orders issued to her. And all of these people from the list, if they are still alive, can confirm that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was your wife told that it would not be a good idea for her to come to work for a while? Wasn't that the way it had been put?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true. They were forbidden from coming back to work ever again. They were not eligible to work any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is she on this list?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, she's not on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you on this list?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I am not on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So she was told after the attack on Prijedor on the 30th not to come to work for a while; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I'd have to ask my wife what date that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, can we say, then, that up until the 25th of May, that is the latest date here, I think, the 25th of May, that up until the 25th of May, both you and your wife had continued to work?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I never received anything officially. I was in camp. No one came to tell me that I was no longer employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that these were Muslims and Croats. Can you read the name under number 11.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Jelena Topic. I said that I did know one Serb. I just mentioned the persons I knew, and among them is Zoran Vikalo, who I know. We were at university together. He's a Serb. He did not want to respond to the call-up, mobilisation. He fled to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Jelena Topic a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at number 19?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read it for us?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Dr. Risto Stojanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, he's probably a Macedonian, Stojanovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 20, please?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dr. Mario Karacic. That is probably a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about 22?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Josipa Grozdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is she a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, she's not, but I just mentioned the people I knew. I don't know what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that this was a list of persons who were dismissed on ethnic grounds; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I said that most of them were dismissed on ethnic grounds or had not responded to mobilisation or had not wanted to do what the Serbs had ordered them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read number 25, and can you tell us whether that lady is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Jozica Djakovic. She is not a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read 38?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Slavica Nukic. She's not a Muslim either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read number 50?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Of course. Dusanka Vuketic. She's not a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: She's a Serb, isn't she?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, you do know full well that Dusanka is a Serb name.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I tell?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read number 60?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Marinko Romanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He's not a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 70?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Jasna Jakovljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is she Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Jasna can be a Muslim name and a Serb name. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Jakovljevic, her last name?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are there any Muslims who have the last name Jakovljevic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: How can I tell? I'm no expert for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, Jakovljevic is based on the name Jakov, which is Jacob, Saint Jacob.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I say?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Emilija Jordan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is she a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Maybe. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Emilija, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Why not? Why not? I mean, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, Doctor, let us be serious. 90?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Vid Djakovic, that's not a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 98? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zoran Vikalo. I mentioned him already. He's a Serb who fled to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about 103?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Ana Juric. That is not a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about 106?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Danica Bijekic, that's not a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dr. Vojislav Milosev, that's not a Muslim name either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And 111?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dubravka Zec. I think that's a Croat name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you come up with that? A Croat with the last name of Zec? What are you saying?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I had a lady who was my friend who was a Croat. Her last name was Zec. How can I tell?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, do you remember that a dismissal is one thing? It has to be accompanied by reasoning, whereas a termination of employment is something else, and the main reason for that is failure to appear for work for five days?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I studied medicine, not law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 16 you said that a certain doctor was taken to Omarska and killed.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were many who were taken to Omarska and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's quite simple. When I got out of the camp, I talked to people. There were some people who came from Omarska, and finally all the bodies have been identified. It is known that those people were taken to Omarska. Their bodies were later found, and they were killed. If you want me to, I can give you some names. You can check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested. You know that from the words of others?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was not there when these people were killed nor would have the Serbs allowed anyone watch them kill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You went on to say that you worked at the medical centre in Prijedor, and you worked at Trnopolje, and it's referred to here as a clinic, but it was not a clinic, was it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was a small village clinic or an infirmary. I was in charge of that infirmary, and at the sawmill in Kozarac I also worked as a substitute doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But your permanent job was at the outpatient clinic in Trnopolje, at this little infirmary.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that some Muslims and Croats were hiding from mobilisation drives. What about the mobilisation in June 1991 or September 1991? Which one were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was after the war in Croatia had already started, and especially after the Serbs with their army took over Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to Prijedor. Now you're talking about JNA mobilisations linked to the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From which mobilisation were they hiding?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean which one? There was only one army, and their military police were -- was looking for people to mobilise them by force and send them to the war in Croatia. When exactly that was going on I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your Brdjanin testimony, 1D04458, page 7 -- sorry, line. The page is 1792, lines 7 to 25, you said that many Muslims were hiding so that the army could not find them and send them to the front lines. You say they were hiding. I want to know which mobilisation drive they were hiding from and for how long.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware that there are two types of mobilisation. Whether it was in September or perhaps in early 1991, I don't know. They were hiding until the conflict in Prijedor broke out. And it was not only the Muslims and Croats who were hiding. There were some Serbs hiding as well. Radenko Djindjic was hiding in a Muslim house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So from June or September onwards, they were hiding from the military police; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For how long were they in hiding and where?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I know that people had a rucksack or a -- ready and packed so that if the military police came they could run to their neighbour's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about their jobs at the time? Did they go to work? Could the military police have found them at work?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Most of them did continue to go to work. Some didn't, perhaps. I know that, later on, all the policemen who did not sign the loyalty statement to the Serbs were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is mobilising conscripts or reservists a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You should ask a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of anyone who was arrested and sent to the front line in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dr. Emir Ceric, caught at his own home, given a uniform and sent to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You should ask him. Fahrudin Bahtijarevic, sent to dig trenches. You can ask him. He's still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the war in Croatia end in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDA or some other party?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in negotiations at any level or were you regularly kept informed about negotiations between different sides in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know only what I heard from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D04459, page 7820, you said that you don't know if anyone was sent to the front line by force, and you cannot provide any names, and now you have given names.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't remember the names at that time, and then when I returned home, I gave it some more thought, and I made inquiries. I cannot memorise all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you are testifying now after making inquiries following previous testimonies so that you can give those names today.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's not true. It's 19 years after the fact today, so it's natural I have to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you rely on your own memory? Can you rely on your memory?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Exact dates are easily forgotten, and names too, but things that really happened remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mention roadblocks, and now you corrected yourself saying that there were roadblocks. And you said also that Muslims also held some check-points of their own.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I said I had seen a check-point at the entrance to Kozarac, but I have to add that in my view, there is a difference between a person who sets up a roadblock in front of their own house to defend their own home and their children and the wife from being raped and someone who sets up a check-point with the intention of killing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the check-point near Kozarac, on the road between Prijedor and Banja Luka, 12 kilometres away from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: If you mean the one held by Muslims, was looking from that road at the entrance to Kozarac, not on the road from Prijedor to Banja Luka but when you approach Kozarac at a distance of about 50 to 100 metres, and on the intersection itself, a Serb tank was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Outside Hambarine was the check-point Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Stakic case, you spoke about that on page 11798. You were asked whether there were any check-points at other places near that road near Kozarusa. You said you didn't know, but you heard that when the Serbs took Prijedor, check-points were set up in Muslim settlements because that was a sign that Serbs were going to take Muslim settlements by force.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Can you show me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The page is 11798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the Brdjanin testimony. And just for Mr. Karadzic's benefit, if the transcript starts 77 or 78, then it's the Stakic testimony. If it starts 117, then it's the Brdjanin testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to upload it now. Do we have that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have 1D04458. 1D04458.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. This is Stakic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I see the translation in our language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, we do not have the translation of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read it and the interpreters were interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what is the 65 ter number first? Yes, we have it. Page 11789.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11798.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Beginning with line 9: "[In English] Whether -- like I was asked whether there were any check-points at other places, outside of this road, perhaps at Kozarusa, I don't know. But I did hear that when the Serb army took over Prijedor and when they were indicating they were going to take the Muslim settlements by force, then non-Serbs, Muslims and Croats, organised themself [sic] -- themselves and put up guards in order to defend themselves, in order to prevent the Serbs from entering the villages suddenly and committing a massacre." [Interpretation] Did you say this?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's possible. That's just what I said about Kozarac a moment ago, that people were defending their families and their houses, not organising themselves to attack Serbs or anyone else and kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what you heard; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we agree to make a distinction between what you heard and what you knew for sure or saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what I saw. Before I went to Kozarac, two days before I left I was living in Old Town, and in the evenings, at night, people stood guard without any weapons, fearing that Serbs may come and kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You lived in the Old Town and worked in Trnopolje; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know why the army took control over Prijedor on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's simple. Just before that, at a session of the parliament, you yourself said that Muslims would disappear from that area, and they have no chance of defending themselves, and, generally speaking, it was a plan to carry out ethnic cleansing and organise a Greater Serbia. And then when it was voted in Bosnia and Herzegovina that Bosnia should be independent and sovereign, whereas you lost at the elections in Prijedor because, as far as I know, the SDA won the elections, you decided to take over by force, and you did it using the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you speaking of my speech of the 15th of October, when I asked that we should refrain from going for independence unless it was agreed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know of only one speech where you said that Muslims had nothing to defend themselves with. They will fail to defend themselves and they would disappear from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I try to talk Muslims into war or not to go to war?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You were the leader of your party, and I know that in reality, Chetnik units were restored and re-established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the speech? In that speech, was I trying to tell Muslims that we shouldn't go to war or that we were going to war?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. You were telling them what awaits them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Chetnik units. Did I set up Chetnik units?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You should know better than anyone else. You come from a family that was a Chetnik family during the Second World War, and you know that in that war Chetniks also wanted a Greater Serbia, and back then there were also killing both Serbs and Croats without any ammunition, preferably by knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My father was in Montenegro where it was not between Serbs and Croats. It was fighting for the king. Why are you bringing my father into this?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm just saying that you know these things better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you said a moment ago that we set up Chetnik units. Did I set them up?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You know that better than I. How would I know? It was organised through the SDA. To what extent you were involved, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you were speaking a moment ago as if you knew about these things, but never mind. Do you know that on the 29th, a dispatcher arrived to Prijedor ordering an attack from the ministry and from the army?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Mr. Karadzic might like to clarify the answer at -- on page 37, line 24, when the interpretation came through that it was the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you meant SDS, it was organised through the SDS. Is it correct, Dr. Merdzanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the reason -- actually, yes. At that moment it was the JNA. Do you know why the JNA took over control over the city, the telegram ordering attack against the JNA, the city, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you denying that the crisis in Hambarine broke out because of the fact that two Serbs were killed and two Croats and two Serbs were wounded? They were reservists, and it was at a check-point near Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that because of shooting at check-points in Kozarac an ultimatum was issued to hand over weapons, not to place badges?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did not attend the negotiations. I knew that the Serbs wanted to take over Kozarac using their own police badges. That was an insignificant matter. They needed some kind of excuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that a curfew was imposed after these killings so that the situation would calm down and that things in general would calm down?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is not true. A curfew was imposed when the army took over Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You knew Sead Cirkin; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I heard of him, and I saw him once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 21st or 22nd of May, you went to Kozarac, and you stayed there. You did not return to Trnopolje; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you placed yourself at the disposal of the persons who were preparing to fight; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is not right. I just organised the infirmary. In case somebody is wounded, we should be able to help. That had nothing to do with anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see, in the Brdjanin case, you said -- actually, you confirm that Cirkin was an active-duty officer and that you went to see him and that you saw a group of young men who were carrying weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you said that since there was this ultimatum to hand over weapons that was running out on the 22nd of May, would you agree that it was not then but a day or two later?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know that the attack started on the 24th. I heard that it was the 22nd, that that was the date. Now, I don't know whether that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that -- that this evidence is also contained in the Stakic case, and I recall Your Honour asking with the previous witness whether information that Mr. Karadzic keeps putting to him from prior transcripts other than the transcript that's in evidence, whether it's also contained in -- in what is now evidence in this case. And I also noted in relation to the mobilisation issue with Muslims and Croats going into hiding where he put the Brdjanin transcript, that's also included in the Stakic transcript, so I don't know whether Your Honour wants to give Mr. Karadzic some guidance in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. I would very much prefer to concentrate on the transcript that has been admitted into evidence in this case, but it's for you, Mr. Karadzic, but bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency, but when I come across contradictions, then I have to refer to his previous statements and testimony. I believe that you would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there's any contradiction between the two transcripts, according to the statement by Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, I would agree. Of course, Mr. Karadzic can take the witness to any alleged inconsistencies between the two transcripts, but in -- in this regard, in relation to Sead Cirkin, transcript page 7723, it says: "He was an active military officer, and I wanted to talk to him," blah, blah, blah. So it's not inconsistent in my view, but I've said what I've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue. And, Mr. Karadzic, yourself as well, please put a pause between the answer and your new question. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did you say that the ultimatum had to do with -- I mean, I'll tell you, this is your statement to the OTP, 2000, 1D4457, page 010352. The ultimatum had to do with hoisting the flag and having insignia on uniforms. That ultimatum was issued by Zupljanin to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's quite possible that I said that, but in principle, no, the policemen in Kozarac were supposed to sign an oath of allegiance to the Serbs, and Kozarac was supposed to be taken over. That was the precondition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the hand-over of weapons and the cease-fire was not a precondition? The people of Kozarac were not supposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the people of Kozarac did not attack anyone. They were just at their homes ready to defend themselves. They did not leave Kozarac. They did not go out to attack the Serbs. It's the Serbs who came to Kozarac to attack the people of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you're saying is on page 7722 in the Stakic case as well. Your amalgamated statement, 7722, from the Stakic case. Yes, 22174, that is the amalgamated statement. On page 7722 you also say that this is an ultimatum that has do with the flag and insignia. Then you say in response to the question put to you in view of negotiations, you said that you thought that they were not successful, and you say: "I heard that Zupljanin did not come to the negotiations," and so on. And in response to the question, "Who did you hear this from?" You said, "I heard this from patients and personnel people who worked there," and so on and so forth. And then they asked you whether you ever heard on radio or television that there was this ultimatum and you say that you had never heard of that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is to say that you don't know about these negotiations and the essence of the ultimatum. You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I never claimed to have been present during these negotiations. I always asserted that I heard all of this, and I can repeat that. It was stated that Stojan Zupljanin had come and had given -- and gave an ultimatum, and Serbs presented an ultimatum to Kozarac and the police. It wasn't the other way around. It was the Serbs who said that they would attack Kozarac if they did not surrender. It's not the other way around as you've been trying to say all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On radio and television, did you hear what was actually said, what the ultimatum had to do with?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You want me to talk about radio and television here now. When the war started in Bosnia, the first thing that the Serbs did was take over radio and TV relay towers so that they could carry out their own propaganda. Radio Prijedor also carried their propaganda. For example, they accused Sikora Mahmuljin --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a minute --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You wait. Let me explain this to you. When they accused them over the radio that they had mistreated Serb patients, they arrested them and took them to Omarska and killed them. On the radio there was this propaganda that the Serbs did not want to have a war. They just wanted to protect all Serbs and Muslims, and at the same time, they went to people's houses, they searched them, and they beat Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Not to go into all of this now. You gathered equipment and medicine and IV liquids and so on before the conflict in Kozarac; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's not the way you put it. There was a pharmacy in Kozarac that had medicine there anyway, prescription medicines. A day before that we went to this pharmacy, and we got medicines from that list, and we took these medicines to the infirmary in Kozarac so that we could have them if we needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who thought of that? Were you the person who thought of that, or did somebody order you to do that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Nobody ordered me to do that. I cannot remember now whether I was the one who thought of that. There were about ten of us there who were discussing this, what to do, how to organise ourselves, because obviously there was an ultimatum there. The police from Kozarac did not want to surrender, and before that, an ultimatum had been issued to Hambarine, and they had torched Hambarine and razed it to the ground. Then we decided since in the infirmary itself, in Kozarac that is, there wasn't enough medicine, then we remembered that pharmacy, and we brought whatever was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the OTP of 2000, on the 27th and 28th of August, in e-court that is 1D04457, on page 01035292, you say, and I'm going to read this out in English -- yes, actually, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will bring it up. 1D4457. We have them in both languages, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have page 01035292. That's probably English. It must be page 3 in e-court, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this, where it says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, now we have both pages in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you find that bit here where you say that you are the staff of this infirmary in Kozarac, that you went to the pharmacy, that you personally went there, that you took this medical equipment as you were expecting an attack, and that you got IV fluids and so on and so forth? Did you do that as a physician who was someone who had passed a test in war surgery?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did not pass any such test. I had just received a degree in medicine, and I had not specialised in anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, we all took this exam in war surgery, didn't we? Within the subject called surgery there is wartime surgery, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any longer. I remember passing that exam called surgery, but I do not remember war surgery, and it had nothing to do with the wounds that we were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In English it's the last paragraph. "[In English] On 23rd of May, 1992, the employees of the clinic, including myself, went to the pharmacy in Kozarac and loaded up on medical supplies, anticipating the attack on Kozarac." [Interpretation] So, Dr. Merdzanic, you did not return to Trnopolje. You stayed in Kozarac. You placed yourself at Cirkin's disposal, and you became his military medical man.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is a pure lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you not go back to work?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: For a simple reason. One reason is the following: After the ultimatum, the Serbs no longer allowed anyone to leave Kozarac. Then there was another reason. Somebody was supposed to help these poor people and treat them medically if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that has nothing to do with Cirkin or any other military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you had prepared all these medical supplies for the attack that was about to take place.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's not true. These medical supplies were in the pharmacy before the war just like in any other civilian pharmacy. That is not correct. You are just trying to plant something on me. Try to be a bit fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state all of this that is contained in this last paragraph that starts with the words: "On the 23rd of May, 1992, the employees the clinic, including myself," et cetera, et cetera, "anticipating the attack on Kozarac."

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not in the context that you have been trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, at transcript page 7724, the witness says: "Kozarac was cut off. There was no one to obtain extra supplies from. The only thing we had was a pharmacy in Kozarac itself, so we took the supplies from the pharmacy and brought all the supplies from the pharmacy to the outpatient clinic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. But I take it that's the part you can raise in your re-examination. We will admit these two pages, English page 3 and 4. I don't know the pages in the B/C/S, but the corresponding page -- pages will be admitted. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exhibit D1922.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at what you said here: "[In English] On one occasion, I went to see Sead Cirkin a few days before the attack, probably about the 20th of May or so. I wanted to talk to him about Cirkin's plan for the GP surgery in the event of attack. He told me that: I will do my job, you do yours. He did not have much time for me. He encouraged me to take care of my surgery myself." [Interpretation] This is midway in the penultimate paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That just confirms my version, namely, that I had no direct connection to Cirkin. As a civilian doctor, I just tried to help civilians in Kozarac as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you did report to the commander, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wanted to see whether he had a plan of any kind. That just confirms that there was no co-ordination between the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you say in 1D4461, page 119 -- sorry, 795, that you only heard of Cirkin, whereas in this statement you say clearly that you made contact with him and talked about his plans. This GP is probably general practice surgery. Where were you telling the truth, when you said you only heard about him or when you said you made contact with him, saw him, and asked him about a plan?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It is indeed written somewhere. I saw Cirkin. I went to see him to ask him if there was a plan of any kind, but I went to see him as a simple civilian without any other intentions that are trying to ascribe to me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second. Yes. Is there a mistake in terms of number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going say Mr. Karadzic is mischaracterising the witness's evidence. That is not what is contained on transcript page 7723.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 7723, lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But he referred to something else, page -- 1D4469, page 11795. Shall we upload it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He said you're making --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] ... I just read is at the bottom of this page, 1D04461. It says: Do you know who Sead Cirkin is? Look at line 20 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
